problems.title: Playlist Heat Segment
problems.story: A community radio station logs the track number of every song it plays during a broadcast day. The day's heat is how many times its most-played track went out. For the evening highlight reel the producer wants the shortest continuous piece of the log that is just as hot as the whole day, so the reel feels like the day did.
problems.statement:
You are given the track numbers in the order they were played.

The heat of a list of plays is the largest number of times any one track number appears in it.

Return the length of the shortest run of consecutive plays whose heat equals the heat of the whole log.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the track number of one play, in the order the plays went out. There is at least one play.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the number of plays in the shortest run that is as hot as the whole log.

parameters.name: plays
parameters.description: The track number of each play, in broadcast order.

constraints: A track number may repeat any number of times

examples.explanation: Track 7 is played three times, more than any other, so the heat is 3. The run must contain all three plays of track 7, which sit at positions 1 and 5, so the shortest such run covers positions 1 to 5: five plays.
Tracks 12 and 5 are each played twice, so the heat is 2. Either track can supply it: 12 needs positions 0 to 2 and 5 needs positions 1 to 3, both three plays long.
A single play has heat 1, and the run made of that one play has heat 1 as well.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Two tracks tie for the heat.
A single play.
The largest track number is the hottest.
Three tracks reach the heat of 3. Track 1, played first, spans seven plays and track 5, the first to reach the heat, spans four, but track 7 spans only three.
Three tracks tie at heat 2; the tightest spans are two plays long, and the first track seen is not one of them.
Every play is the same track.
Heat 1: any single play is as hot as the day.
Nine thousand plays over three hundred tracks.

hints: The heat of the whole log is fixed. Which tracks could possibly give a short run that heat?
A run is only as hot as the day if it contains every play of one of the hottest tracks.
For each track, remember where it was first played, where it was last played and how often. The shortest answer among the hottest tracks is last minus first plus one.

editorial.overview: A run reaches the day's heat only if some single track is played inside it as often as it was played all day, which means the run contains every play of that track. So the answer is decided track by track: for each hottest track, the shortest run is the stretch from its first play to its last. This is a frequency-counting problem over a hash map.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try every run, count the plays of each track inside it, and keep the shortest run whose largest count equals the day's heat. That is O(n^2) runs with counting on top, far too slow for two hundred thousand plays.
editorial.optimalApproach: Walk the log once with a hash map from track number to its first position and its count so far. When a track's count reaches c at position i, the stretch from its first play to i is the shortest run containing c plays of it. Keep the best pair seen: a larger count wins, and an equal count wins if its stretch is shorter. After the walk the stored length is the answer.
editorial.correctnessProof: Let H be the day's heat. Any run of heat H contains H plays of some track t, and t is played only H times in total, so the run contains all of t's plays and is at least as long as t's span from first to last play. Conversely, the span of any hottest track has heat exactly H: it contains H plays of that track and no track can appear more than H times. So the answer is the minimum span over hottest tracks. The single pass computes each track's span at the moment its count reaches its final value, and the comparison keeps the minimum span among tracks with the largest count.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n) expected with a hash map.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(d) for the distinct track numbers.

problems.title: Tour Bus Cuisine Stretch
problems.story: A food-walk guide leads tourists down a street of stalls, and every stall cooks one cuisine. The guide has prepared notes on only a few cuisines, so the walk has to be a continuous stretch of the street on which every stall cooks one of at most that many cuisines. The longer the walk, the better the tour sells.
problems.statement:
You are given how many cuisines the guide can talk about, followed by the cuisine code of every stall in order along the street.

A walk is a run of neighbouring stalls. It is allowed when the stalls on it cook at most that many different cuisines.

Return the number of stalls on the longest allowed walk. If the guide can talk about no cuisines at all, no stall can be visited and the answer is 0.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is how many different cuisines the guide can talk about. Every number after it is the cuisine code of one stall, in street order. There is at least one stall.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the number of stalls on the longest allowed walk.

parameters.name: stalls
parameters.description: The cuisine code of each stall, in order along the street.

parameters.name: kinds
parameters.description: How many different cuisines a walk may include.

examples.explanation: With two cuisines allowed, the stalls 3 1 3 3 at the start form a walk of four, and so do 3 3 2 2 in the middle. Any five neighbouring stalls include three cuisines.
With one cuisine allowed the walk must stay on a single cuisine, and the longest such run is the three stalls cooking 6.
Three cuisines are allowed but the street only has two stalls, so the whole street is one walk of two.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Only one cuisine allowed.
No cuisines allowed: nothing can be visited.
The largest allowance and the extreme codes.

When a third cuisine arrives the window must shrink from the left only as far as needed. Restarting the walk at the new stall finds only 3 3 3 1 1, five stalls; keeping the 1 just before it gives six.
One cuisine throughout, well under the allowance.
Every stall differs, so every allowed walk is two stalls.
Nine thousand stalls in runs of repeated cuisines.

hints: If a walk is allowed, every shorter walk inside it is allowed too. That is what lets a window slide.
Grow the walk one stall at a time on the right. When it holds one cuisine too many, which end should give way?
Keep a count per cuisine inside the window. Move the left end forward, decrementing counts, until the number of cuisines with a positive count is back within the allowance.

editorial.overview: Allowed walks are closed under shrinking, so for every right end there is a leftmost start that still works, and that start never moves backwards as the right end advances. That monotonicity is the sliding-window pattern with a hash map counting each cuisine inside the window.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Check every pair of ends, counting distinct cuisines in between, and keep the longest pair within the allowance. That is O(n^2) pairs, too slow for two hundred thousand stalls.
editorial.optimalApproach: Move a right pointer across the street, adding each stall's cuisine to a count map and noting when a count goes from zero to one. While more cuisines than allowed are present, remove the stall at the left pointer and advance it, noting when a count drops to zero. After each step the window is the longest allowed walk ending at the right pointer; keep the largest width seen.
editorial.correctnessProof: Let L(r) be the smallest start such that stalls L(r)..r form an allowed walk. Because removing stalls never adds a cuisine, every start after L(r) also works, and L(r+1) >= L(r): if a start before L(r) failed for right end r, adding stall r+1 cannot fix it. The algorithm keeps the invariant that after processing r the left pointer equals L(r), since it advances only while the window is not allowed and stops at the first start that is. The answer is the maximum of r - L(r) + 1 over all r, which is exactly what is recorded. With an allowance of zero every window shrinks to empty and the answer is zero.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n) expected: each stall enters and leaves the window once.

problems.title: Bakery Oven Rate
problems.story: A neighbourhood bakery has one oven and a list of loaf orders due before the morning opening. The oven bakes in hour-long rounds, and each round can only hold loaves for a single order. A faster oven setting burns more gas, so the baker wants the slowest setting that still clears every order before opening time.
problems.statement:
You are given the number of hours before opening, followed by how many loaves each order needs.

At a setting of r, one hour-long round bakes up to r loaves for one order. An order of x loaves therefore takes x divided by r rounds, rounded up: the last round of an order may be only partly used, and the leftover space cannot be given to another order.

Return the smallest whole-number setting at which all the orders together take no more hours than are available. There are always at least as many hours as orders, so some setting always works.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is the hours available before opening. Every number after it is the loaf count of one order. There is at least one order.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the smallest oven setting that finishes every order in time.

parameters.name: orders
parameters.description: How many loaves each order needs.

examples.explanation: At setting 5 the orders take 1, 3 and 2 rounds, six hours in all, which fits. At setting 4 they take 1, 4 and 3 rounds, eight hours, which does not.
Three orders and three hours leave one round per order, so the setting must cover the largest order, 9. At setting 8 the order of 9 alone needs two rounds.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
One round per order.
One order and one hour: the whole order must fit in one round.
As many hours as loaves: the slowest setting works, and the hour count reaches its limit.
Two huge orders, one round each.
Settings 4 and 5 still leave every order needing two rounds, six hours in all, one more than available. Rounding the division down instead of up accepts them.
The answer sits strictly between the smallest and largest order.
Equal orders and twice as many hours as orders.
Five and a half thousand orders up to a billion loaves each.

hints: If a setting finishes on time, does every faster setting also finish on time?
That yes means you can search for the answer instead of trying every setting from 1 upward.
Binary search the setting between 1 and the largest order. For each candidate, add up the rounded-up rounds per order and compare with the hours.

editorial.overview: The hours needed only fall as the setting rises, so the settings that work form a range that starts at the answer and runs upward. Binary search on the answer finds where that range begins, with a linear check of each candidate.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try settings 1, 2, 3 and so on until one fits. With orders of a billion loaves that can take a billion checks, each over every order.
editorial.optimalApproach: Search the setting r in [1, max order]. The largest order is always enough, because it gives every order a single round and there are at least as many hours as orders. For a candidate r, compute the total of ceil(x / r) over the orders as (x + r - 1) / r in integer arithmetic, and stop early if it already exceeds the hours. If the total fits, the answer is r or smaller; otherwise it is larger. The totals stay below 10^14, inside 64-bit and exact double range.
editorial.correctnessProof: For every order, ceil(x / r) is non-increasing in r, so the total hours T(r) is non-increasing too. Hence the set of settings with T(r) <= hours is an upward-closed interval [r*, max]. It is non-empty because T(max) equals the number of orders, which is at most the hours. Binary search over a monotone predicate returns the smallest r with T(r) <= hours, which is r* by definition.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n log M), where M is the largest order.

problems.title: Ridge Line Lows
problems.story: A surveyor walks a ridge and records the ground height at evenly spaced posts. For flood planning, any stretch of neighbouring posts is rated by its lowest post, because that is where run-off would pool. The planning office wants one number that weighs every possible stretch at once: the total of the lows of all of them.
problems.statement:
You are given the height at each post, in order along the ridge.

A stretch is any run of one or more neighbouring posts, and its low is the smallest height in it. A ridge of n posts has n times (n + 1) / 2 stretches.

Return the sum of the lows of every stretch. The sum can be very large, so return it modulo 1000000007.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the height of one post, in order along the ridge. There is at least one post.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the total of the lows of all stretches, modulo 1000000007.

parameters.name: heights
parameters.description: The ground height at each post, in order along the ridge.

examples.explanation: The six stretches are 6, 2, 5, 6 2, 2 5 and 6 2 5. Their lows are 6, 2, 5, 2, 2 and 2, which add up to 19.
The stretches are the first post, the second post and both together. Each has a low of 4, so the total is 12. Equal heights must not be counted twice for the pair.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Two equal posts.
One post: its single stretch has a low of 614.
Six stretches with a low of a billion: the plain total is six billion and must be reduced.
All equal. Treating ties as strictly smaller on both sides counts some stretches twice; on neither side, not at all.
A rising ridge: each post is the low only of stretches that start at it.
Lows that reign over different spans to each side.
Close to six thousand posts near the height limit.

hints: Instead of visiting every stretch, ask the question the other way round: for one post, how many stretches is it the low of?
A post is the low of a stretch when nothing in the stretch is lower. How far can the stretch reach to the left and to the right?
Find, for every post, the nearest lower post on each side with a monotonic stack. Break ties on one side only, so a stretch with two equal lows is credited to exactly one of them.

editorial.overview: Summing over stretches is quadratic, but every stretch has a low, so the total can be regrouped by which post supplies that low. Each post's share is its height times the number of stretches it rules, and those counts come from the nearest lower neighbour on each side, which a monotonic stack finds in linear time.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Fix each start, extend the end one post at a time while tracking the running minimum, and add it. That is O(n^2), about five billion steps at the largest size.
editorial.optimalApproach: Credit each stretch to its leftmost lowest post. For post i, let left be the distance back to the previous post with height at most h[i] (or to the start), and right the distance forward to the next post with height strictly less than h[i] (or to the end). Post i is the credited low of exactly left times right stretches. One stack pass from the left gives every left distance (pop while the top is higher), one from the right gives every right distance (pop while the top is at least as high). Add h[i] times left times right, reducing modulo 1000000007 after each multiplication so that no product leaves 64-bit range.
editorial.correctnessProof: Every stretch has a unique leftmost position holding its minimum, so crediting each stretch to that position counts it exactly once. A stretch [l, r] is credited to i exactly when l <= i <= r, every post in [l, i - 1] is strictly higher than h[i], and every post in [i + 1, r] is at least h[i]. The valid l run from just after the previous post with height at most h[i] up to i, which is left choices, and the valid r run from i up to just before the next strictly lower post, which is right choices; the choices are independent. Summing h[i] times left times right therefore equals the sum of all lows. The stacks are correct because a post that is popped can never be the nearest qualifying neighbour of any later post.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n): every post is pushed and popped at most once per pass.
editorial.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the stacks and the distances.

python3.referenceSolution:
def sumOfLows(heights: list[int]) -> int:
    mod = 1_000_000_007
    n = len(heights)
    left = [0] * n
    right = [0] * n
    stack = []
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] > heights[i]:
            stack.pop()
        left[i] = i - (stack[-1] if stack else -1)
        stack.append(i)
    stack = []
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        while stack and heights[stack[-1]] >= heights[i]:
            stack.pop()
        right[i] = (stack[-1] if stack else n) - i
        stack.append(i)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):
        total = (total + heights[i] % mod * left[i] % mod * right[i]) % mod
    return total

problems.title: Clue Trail Loop
problems.story: A scavenger hunt is laid out on numbered clue cards. Each card tells the player which card to read next, or that the hunt is over. After a playtest the organisers suspect that a miswritten card sends players round in circles forever, and they want to know how many cards that circle holds before they reprint any.
problems.statement:
You are given, for every card, the number of the card it sends the player to next, or -1 if that card ends the hunt. Cards are numbered from 0, and the hunt starts at card 0.

Follow the trail from card 0. If it reaches a card that ends the hunt, return 0. Otherwise the trail eventually repeats a card and goes round the same loop forever; return the number of different cards on that loop.

Cards the trail from card 0 never reaches do not matter, even if they form loops of their own.
problems.inputFormat: The number at position i, counting positions from 0, is the card that card i sends the player to, or -1 if card i ends the hunt. There is at least one card.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the number of cards on the loop the trail falls into, or 0 if the hunt ends.

parameters.name: nextCard
parameters.description: For each card, the card it points to next, or -1 when it ends the hunt.

constraints: A card may point to itself
A solution using constant extra memory exists

examples.explanation: The trail runs 0, 2, 3, 4 and then back to 2. Cards 2, 3 and 4 form the loop, so the answer is 3. Card 0 is on the way in but not on the loop, and card 1 is never visited.
The trail runs 0, 3, 1, and card 1 ends the hunt. Card 2 points back to 0, but the trail never reaches card 2.
Card 0 sends the player to card 2, and card 2 sends the player back to itself: a loop of one card.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
The hunt ends.
A single card that ends the hunt.
A card that points to itself.
Cards 1 and 2 form a loop, but the trail ends at card 0. Scanning every card for loops answers 2.
The loop is the whole deck, including card 0 itself.
A long tail into a loop of one card at the end.
A long tail into a loop of three thousand and one cards, with a decoy loop nobody reaches.
Six of the eight cards send the player to card 3, so one target repeats again and again. The trail runs 0, 3, 4, 5 and back to 3: a loop of three cards.

hints: Each card has exactly one next card, so this is a singly linked list that may end or may bend back on itself.
Two walkers on the trail, one taking two steps for every one the other takes, meet if and only if there is a loop.
Once they meet you are standing on the loop. Walk around it from there until you return, counting cards.

editorial.overview: The cards form a linked list stored as an array of next pointers, starting at card 0. Either it ends at -1 or it enters a cycle. Floyd's fast-and-slow pointers detect the cycle in constant memory, and one lap from the meeting point measures it.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Walk the trail, recording the step at which each card was first visited. When a card repeats, the loop length is the current step minus the recorded step. This is linear time but uses memory proportional to the trail, which the constant-memory approach avoids.
editorial.optimalApproach: Start slow and fast at card 0. Each round, slow moves one card and fast moves two; if either reaches -1 the hunt ends and the answer is 0. If they ever stand on the same card, that card is on the loop. Count the loop by stepping from it until it comes back round.
editorial.correctnessProof: If the trail ends, fast reaches -1 first and the answer 0 is correct. If the trail has a tail of length t and a loop of length c, both walkers are on the loop after at most t rounds, and from then on the gap between them, measured along the loop, shrinks by one each round, so they meet within c further rounds. Their meeting card is on the loop, and walking from any loop card returns to it after exactly c steps, which is the number of distinct cards on the loop. Cards not reachable from card 0 are never visited, so their loops cannot affect the answer.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n): at most a tail plus two laps.

problems.title: Archive Index Depth
problems.story: A county archive keeps its catalogue index as a plain binary search tree. Each new accession number is filed in arrival order by the textbook rule: start at the root, go left when smaller and right otherwise, and attach where the path runs out. Re-filed items can repeat a number, and a repeat simply goes right. Nobody ever rebalances it. A lookup costs one step per level, so before the next audit the archivist wants to know how deep the index has grown.
problems.statement:
You are given the accession numbers in the order they were filed. A number can appear more than once.

Insert them one by one into an initially empty binary search tree. The first number becomes the root. Each later number starts at the root and moves to the left child when it is smaller than the current node and to the right child otherwise, that is when it is larger or equal, until the child it needs is missing; it is attached there.

Return the height of the finished tree: the number of nodes on its longest path from the root down to a leaf.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is one accession number, in the order it was filed. Numbers may repeat, and there is at least one.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path of the finished tree.

parameters.name: keys
parameters.description: The accession numbers in filing order. Numbers may repeat.

constraints: Keys may repeat; an equal key goes to the right
Filing in sorted order is allowed, so the tree may be a single path

examples.explanation: 40 is the root, 22 and 63 its children, and the last four fill the level below. Every leaf is three nodes from the top.
Each number is smaller than everything before it, so each one hangs to the left of the last. The tree is a single path of five nodes.
20 goes right of 10, and 15 goes right of 10 and then left of 20, so the path 10, 20, 15 has three nodes.
Each repeat of 5 goes right of the 5 before it, so the three filings form a single path of three nodes.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
A single leftward path.
One accession number.
A zig-zag: every insertion goes one level deeper even though the keys alternate between small and large.
The deepest key, 52, has its in-order predecessor 50 and successor 55 at different depths; the parent is the deeper one. Using only one neighbour undercounts.
The extreme key values.
Nine thousand keys in rising order: the tree is one path. Simulating the insertions costs about forty million steps; a recursive insert also overflows a shallow stack.
Five and a half thousand keys spread across the whole range.
Repeats of one number form a rightward path.
The second 10 goes right of the root, 15 right of that, the third 10 left of 15, and 12 right of the third 10: five levels. Treating equal keys as smaller, or skipping them, gives a different height.

hints: Simulating the insertions is correct but can cost a full path walk per key. Filing in sorted order makes every walk as long as the tree.
Where does a new key end up? Think about the keys already in the tree that sit immediately below and above it in sorted order.
A new key becomes the child of either its in-order predecessor or its in-order successor among the earlier keys, and its depth is one more than the deeper of the two.

Those neighbours can be found offline: sort the keys, breaking ties by filing order, link them in a doubly linked list, and remove keys in reverse filing order. At the moment a key is removed, its list neighbours are exactly its predecessor and successor among the keys filed before it.
A repeat goes right of an equal key, so it behaves exactly like a slightly larger key. Breaking ties by filing position turns equal keys into distinct ones without changing the tree.

editorial.overview: The tree's shape is fully determined by the filing order, so the task is to find every node's depth without walking the tree. The key fact is that a newly filed key always hangs under its in-order predecessor or successor among the keys filed before it, whichever is deeper. Finding those neighbours for every key is a classic offline trick with a doubly linked list over the sorted order. Repeated numbers need no special case: a repeat goes right, so ordering keys by value and then by filing position makes every key distinct without changing the tree.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Insert each key by walking from the root, and track the deepest attachment. That is O(n * height), which is O(n^2) when the keys arrive sorted: five billion steps at the largest size.
editorial.optimalApproach: Sort the keys by value, breaking ties by filing position, and give each its rank. Link the ranks in a doubly linked list. Walk the filing order backwards: for the key filed at position i, its current list neighbours are its predecessor and successor among keys filed at positions before i; record them, then unlink the key. Then walk the filing order forwards, setting depth(key) = 1 + max(depth(predecessor), depth(successor)), with a missing neighbour counting as depth 0. The height is the largest depth.
editorial.correctnessProof: Compare keys by value and then by filing position. A repeat goes right of an equal node, exactly as a slightly larger key would, so the tree is a binary search tree over these distinct pairs and the argument below applies to it unchanged. Let p and s be the nearest smaller and larger keys among those filed before k; either may be missing. No earlier key lies strictly between them, so one is an ancestor of the other: the lowest common ancestor of two keys in a binary search tree lies between them in value, and here it can only be p or s itself. Call the deeper of the two q. Every comparison on the search path for k comes out the same as it would for any value strictly between p and s, so the search reaches q. And q has no child on k's side, because that child would hold a key strictly between p and s. So k is attached directly under q, and its depth is one more than the larger of the two depths; with one neighbour missing the same argument uses the other, and with both missing k is the root. The backward pass finds p and s correctly because, when the key filed at position i is unlinked, the list holds exactly the keys filed at positions 0 to i, so its list neighbours are its neighbours among earlier keys.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n log n) for the sort; both passes are linear.

python3.referenceSolution:
def treeHeight(keys: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(keys)
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: (keys[i], i))
    rank = [0] * n
    for r, i in enumerate(order):
        rank[i] = r
    prev = list(range(-1, n - 1))
    nxt = list(range(1, n + 1))
    pred = [-1] * n
    succ = [-1] * n
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        r = rank[i]
        p, s = prev[r], nxt[r]
        pred[i] = p
        succ[i] = s if s < n else -1
        if p >= 0:
            nxt[p] = s
        if s < n:
            prev[s] = p
    depth = [0] * n
    best = 0
    for i in range(n):
        d = 1
        if pred[i] >= 0:
            d = max(d, depth[pred[i]] + 1)
        if succ[i] >= 0:
            d = max(d, depth[succ[i]] + 1)
        depth[rank[i]] = d
        best = max(best, d)
    return best

problems.title: Ferry Ticket Change
problems.story: The river ferry's ticket booth sells one fare, 5 coins, and passengers pay with 5, 10 or 20 coin notes. The booth opens every morning with an empty cash box, so all the change it hands out comes from notes earlier passengers paid with. The first passenger who cannot be given exact change closes the sale for the crossing.
problems.statement:
You are given the note each passenger pays with, in queue order. Every note is 5, 10 or 20, and every passenger buys one ticket at 5.

A passenger paying 5 needs no change. A passenger paying 10 must be given one 5. A passenger paying 20 must be given 15, either as a 10 and a 5 or as three 5s. Change can only be made from notes already taken in. Twenty-coin notes are never given as change.

Sell in queue order, choosing how to give change as well as possible. Return how many passengers buy a ticket before the first one who cannot be given change, or the whole queue if nobody is turned away.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the note one passenger pays with, in queue order: 5, 10 or 20. There is at least one passenger.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: how many passengers buy a ticket before the sale has to stop.

parameters.name: notes
parameters.description: The note each passenger pays with, in queue order; each is 5, 10 or 20.

examples.explanation: The first 5 goes in the box and becomes the change for the 10. The second 5 goes in, and the 20 is given that 5 and the 10: everyone is served.
The second passenger needs 15 in change, but the box holds a single 5. The sale stops after one ticket, even though the third passenger pays exactly.
The very first passenger needs a 5 back and the box is empty, so no tickets are sold.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
Turned away at the second passenger.
One passenger with a 20 and an empty box.
Paying the 20 with three 5s leaves one 5 and strands the next two 10s after six sales. Paying it with the 10 and a 5 serves all eight.
With no 10 in the box, three 5s are the only way to change the 20; then the 10 cannot be changed.
Nobody needs change.
Fifteen thousand passengers whose notes can all be changed, followed by three paying 10.

hints: Only the counts of 5s and 10s in the box matter. Twenties never come back out.
The only real choice is how to change a 20. Which note is more useful to keep for later passengers, a 5 or a 10?
A 5 can change both a 10 and a 20, but a 10 only helps with a 20. So pay a 20 with a 10 and a 5 whenever you can, and fall back to three 5s.

editorial.overview: The booth's state is just how many 5s and 10s it holds, and the only decision is how to change a 20. Keeping 5s is always at least as good as keeping 10s, so the greedy rule is to spend a 10 first. With that rule the simulation is a single pass.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try both ways of changing every 20 and keep the branch that serves the most passengers. That doubles the work at every 20 and is exponential.
editorial.optimalApproach: Keep two counters. A 5 adds to the fives. A 10 needs a five: take it and add a ten, or stop. A 20 takes a ten and a five if both are there, otherwise three fives, otherwise the sale stops. Return the number of passengers handled before stopping, or the queue length.
editorial.correctnessProof: Compare the two ways of changing a 20 when both are possible: one leaves (f - 1, t - 1) and the other (f - 3, t). Any later sequence of sales possible from (f - 3, t) is possible from (f - 1, t - 1), because wherever the other branch spends its extra 10, this branch can spend two of its extra 5s instead, and wherever it spends a 5, this branch has at least as many. So the greedy state dominates, and by induction over the queue the greedy simulation serves at least as many passengers as any other choice of change, and never more than is possible.

problems.title: Portal Tile Corridor
problems.story: An escape room's final corridor is a single row of painted floor tiles. A player may step onto the tile directly ahead or behind, or step onto a portal pad and reappear on any other tile of the same colour. The designers time the room by its par: the fewest moves that carry a player from the entrance tile to the exit tile.
problems.statement:
You are given the colour of each tile, from the entrance tile to the exit tile.

From tile i a player may make one move to tile i - 1 or tile i + 1, if that tile exists, or to any other tile whose colour equals the colour of tile i.

Return the fewest moves that take a player from the first tile to the last. A corridor of one tile needs no moves.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the colour of one tile, in order from the entrance to the exit. Colours may be negative. There is at least one tile.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the fewest moves from the first tile to the last.

parameters.name: colours
parameters.description: The colour of each tile, from the entrance tile to the exit tile.

constraints: Any number of tiles may share a colour

examples.explanation: One fastest route: portal from tile 0 to tile 3, which is also colour 7, then step to tiles 4, 5 and 6. Stepping along tiles 0, 1, 2, portalling from 2 to 5 and stepping to 6 is four moves as well.
The first and last tiles are both colour 5, so a single portal move finishes the corridor.
The entrance tile is also the exit tile, so the player is already there.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
One portal move.
A single tile.
Extreme colours, alternating.
No colour repeats, so only steps are possible: seven moves.
The best route portals from tile 0 to tile 8 and steps once, two moves. Searching depth-first, or always preferring the forward step, finds longer routes first.
Ten thousand tiles of one colour and a different exit tile.
Five thousand tiles: half with unique colours, half from fifty colours.
Two colours alternate along the corridor, each on many tiles. One step to tile 1, which shares colour 5 with the exit, then one portal: two moves.

hints: Moves all cost the same, so the fewest moves is a shortest path in an unweighted graph. Which search finds those?
Listing every portal as an edge can create a number of edges that grows with the square of the corridor. Group the tiles by colour instead.

In a breadth-first search, the first time any tile of a colour is taken off the queue, every other tile of that colour can be reached in one more move. After that, the colour's group never needs to be looked at again.

editorial.overview: Tiles are nodes and moves are unit-cost edges, so breadth-first search from the first tile gives the answer. The only difficulty is the portal edges, which can number in the hundreds of millions if one colour is common. Expanding each colour group exactly once keeps the search linear.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Run breadth-first search, and from each tile scan every tile of the same colour. When most tiles share a colour that is quadratic: about forty million checks for ten thousand tiles, and over a billion at the largest size.
editorial.optimalApproach: Build a map from colour to the list of tiles with that colour. Breadth-first search from tile 0. When a tile is dequeued, enqueue its unvisited left and right neighbours, and, if its colour's list has not been used yet, enqueue every unvisited tile on that list and mark the colour used. Stop when the last tile is dequeued.
editorial.correctnessProof: Breadth-first search with unit edges dequeues tiles in order of distance from tile 0, so the distance recorded for the last tile is the fewest moves, provided every edge out of a dequeued tile is considered. Neighbour edges always are. For portal edges, let u be the first tile of colour c to be dequeued, at distance d. Every other tile of colour c is reached from u with one move, so each gets distance at most d + 1, and its true distance is at least d + 1 unless it was already found. Any later tile v of colour c is dequeued at distance at least d, so its portal edges could only offer distance d + 1 or more to tiles that already have at most d + 1. Skipping the group for v therefore loses nothing.
editorial.timeComplexity: O(n) expected: each tile is enqueued once and each colour group is scanned once.

problems.title: Mosaic Odd Tile
problems.story: A mosaic kit ships its tiles in matched pairs, each pair stamped with the same pattern number on the back. At the factory one tile lost its twin, so every kit now holds exactly one unmatched tile. The packing line can only afford a single pass over the tiles and a scratch note too small to remember which patterns it has already seen.
problems.statement:
You are given the pattern number stamped on each tile of a kit, in the order the tiles come off the line.

Every pattern number appears on exactly two tiles, except one pattern number that appears on exactly one tile.

Return the pattern number of the unmatched tile. Aim to use only a constant amount of extra memory.
problems.inputFormat: Every number is the pattern number on one tile, in the order the tiles were packed. There is an odd number of tiles, at least one.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the pattern number that appears on only one tile.

parameters.name: tiles
parameters.description: The pattern number on each tile; every value appears twice except one.

constraints: Exactly one pattern number appears once; every other appears exactly twice

examples.explanation: 14 and 3 each appear on two tiles. Pattern 9 appears on only one, so it is the unmatched tile.
A kit of a single tile: that tile is the unmatched one.
Pattern 21 is paired, so the unmatched tile carries pattern 0. Zero is a real pattern number here, not a sign that nothing was found.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
The unmatched pattern is 0.
One tile.
Pattern numbers near the limit.
The unmatched tile comes last.
The unmatched tile comes first.
Sorting and comparing neighbours in pairs must not run off the end when the unmatched value sorts last.
Over five thousand tiles with pattern numbers across the whole range.
Every pair sits side by side, including 0 0 and the largest pattern number. Only 17 has no twin.

hints: A count per pattern number works, but the packing line has no room to remember what it has seen.
Is there an operation that undoes itself when applied twice with the same value, and does not care about order?
Exclusive or: x ^ x is 0, x ^ 0 is x, and it is commutative and associative. Combine every tile and the pairs cancel.

editorial.overview: Paired values have to cancel and the lone value has to survive, in a single pass with constant memory. Bitwise exclusive or does exactly that, which makes this the standard bit-manipulation pattern for finding the one value without a partner.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Count each pattern number in a hash map and return the one with a count of one. That is linear time but needs memory for every distinct pattern.
editorial.optimalApproach: Start from 0 and exclusive-or every pattern number into it. Return the result. All pattern numbers are below 2^31, so this is safe even where the language does bitwise operations on 32-bit integers.
editorial.correctnessProof: Exclusive or is commutative and associative, so the result equals the exclusive or of the values regrouped so that each pair sits together. Each pair contributes x ^ x = 0, and 0 ^ y = y, so what remains is the lone pattern number.

problems.title: Spice Trader Voyages
problems.story: A spice merchant has been told the price a sack of saffron will fetch at the port on each of the coming days. Her ship carries one sack at a time, so she buys on one day and sells on a later one, and every buy-then-sell is one voyage. Her trading licence allows only so many voyages this season, so she wants to know the most she can make.
problems.statement:
You are given the number of voyages the licence allows, followed by the price of a sack on each day in order.

A voyage buys one sack on some day and sells it on the same or a later day. She can hold at most one sack at a time, so a voyage must be sold before the next one is bought; selling one sack and buying the next on the same day is allowed. She may make fewer voyages than allowed, or none.

Return the largest total profit: the sum over all voyages of the selling price minus the buying price.
problems.inputFormat: The first number is how many voyages the licence allows. Every number after it is the price of a sack on one day, in day order. There is at least one day.
problems.outputFormat: Return one integer: the largest total profit, which is never negative.

parameters.name: prices
parameters.description: The price of a sack on each day, in day order.

parameters.name: trades
parameters.description: The largest number of voyages the licence allows.

examples.explanation: Buy at 3 and sell at 8 for 5, then buy at 1 and sell at 7 for 6. Two voyages, total 11.
With one voyage the best single buy and later sell is 1 then 7, worth 6, which beats 3 then 8, worth 5.
No voyages are allowed, so nothing can be earned even though the price rises.

testCases.explanation: The worked example.
One voyage only.
One day: a voyage that buys and sells the same day earns nothing.
A huge allowance and the extreme prices.
Three rises are on offer but only two voyages. Dropping the smallest rise gives 4 + 7 = 11; merging the first two rises into one voyage, 1 to 7, and then 2 to 9 gives 13.
Prices only fall: the best is to make no voyage.
A flat price earns nothing.
A thousand days and three hundred voyages.

hints: On any day she is in one of two situations: holding a sack or not. What else must you know to decide what she can still do?
Track, for each number of voyages started so far, the best cash she can have while holding a sack and while not holding one.
Update each day: holding after buying today is the best not-holding value with one fewer voyage, minus today's price; not holding after selling today is the best holding value plus today's price.
Once the allowance reaches half the number of days, it no longer binds: take every day-to-day rise.

editorial.overview: The choice on each day depends on whether a sack is held and how many voyages have been used, so the state is (voyages, holding). Dynamic programming over that state, one day at a time, gives the best profit in O(days times voyages). When voyages are plentiful the limit stops mattering and the answer is the sum of every rise.
editorial.bruteForceApproach: Try every way to choose non-overlapping buy and sell days with at most the allowed number of pairs. The number of choices grows exponentially with the number of days.
editorial.optimalApproach: If the allowance is at least half the number of days, return the sum of max(0, p[i+1] - p[i]), since no more voyages than that can ever be profitable. Otherwise keep hold[t] and free[t] for t = 1..allowance: the best cash after starting t voyages while holding, and while not holding. For each price p and each t in increasing order, set hold[t] = max(hold[t], free[t-1] - p) and then free[t] = max(free[t], hold[t] + p). The answer is free[allowance], with free[0] = 0 throughout. Profits stay below 10^9.
editorial.correctnessProof: By induction over days, hold[t] and free[t] are the best cash over all valid histories up to the current day that have started t voyages and do or do not hold a sack. A history ends a day either unchanged from the day before, which the max with the old value covers, or having bought today, which must follow a non-holding state with t - 1 voyages, or having sold today, which must follow a holding state with t voyages. Updating t in increasing order lets a same-day sell-then-buy reuse today's free[t-1], which the statement allows. Since free[t] is non-decreasing in t, free[allowance] is the best over all histories with at most the allowance. When the allowance is at least half the days, any optimal plan can be split into one voyage per rising day pair, and there are at most that many, so the limit never binds and the sum of rises is optimal.
